1:
The occasion is the assembly at Gilgal. Gill places the speech there, after the people had recognised Saul and he was established in the kingdom, and while they were in the midst of their mirth and joy. Clarke thinks it very likely the address was delivered at that meeting, no other time being given for it and this the most proper that could be chosen. Wesley makes the timing deliberate and reads it as evidence of Samuel's wisdom: he would not reprove the people for the sin of desiring a king while Saul was unsettled in his kingdom, lest through their accustomed levity they should cast off their king as hastily as they had passionately desired him. He chose this season because Saul's kingdom was now confirmed by an eminent victory, and because the people were rejoicing and applauding themselves for their desires of a king and interpreting the success God had given them as a divine approbation of those desires. Samuel therefore thought fit to temper their joys and excite the repentance he saw wanting in them, which he knew was needed to prevent the curse of God upon their new king and the whole kingdom.

What the address accomplishes Keil and Delitzsch state plainly: with it Samuel closed the solemn confirmation of Saul and handed over the office of judge, which he had hitherto filled, to the king whom God had appointed and the people had joyfully recognised. But the good Israel expected from a king depended entirely on both people and king keeping that attitude towards the LORD with which Israel's prosperity was always bound up, and this is the truth the prophet felt impelled to press on them — reminding them that neither he in the administration of his office nor the LORD in his leading of Israel thus far had given them any reason to ask for a king when the Ammonites invaded.

Ellicott dwells on what kind of document this is. He believes the compiler has preserved many of the very words spoken, a true and detailed account of the day that was the real inauguration of the earthly monarchy — that change in the life of Israel which became of vast importance in the generations after. The speaker belonged to both the old order and the new, the link joining the judges to the kings, men like Gideon and Jephthah, half-veiled in the mists that gather round an unlettered past, with men like David and Solomon round whose lives no mist will ever gather; and words from such a man, who by Israel's cherished tradition was the accredited minister of the invisible King when the Eternal made over the sovereignty, would surely be treasured with jealous care. The chapter, Ellicott adds, has the form of a dialogue between prophet and elders, and the old judge presents the king under the title of the Anointed of the Eternal.

The opening claim is a claim of obedience, and Ellicott sends the reader back to the deputation at Ramah for it (1 Samuel 8:7; 1 Samuel 8:22): the wishes the people expressed on that public occasion had been scrupulously carried out. Henry puts the sentence into Samuel's mouth with the sting left in — I have hearkened to your voice in all that you said to me, desirous to please you if possible and make you easy, though to the discarding of myself and my family; and now will you hearken to me and take my advice? The change was perfected, and the king now walked before them, in public and ready for public business; but Henry turns that into a warning. Now that they had made themselves like the nations in their civil government and cast off the divine administration there, they should take heed not to make themselves like the nations in religion and cast off the worship of God.
2:
The phrase about the king walking before them concerns office, and all read it as a transfer of command. Ellicott has Samuel pointing to Saul at his side, and takes the term to cover the guiding and governing of the people as well as the leading of them in war: henceforth they must accept his authority on all occasions, not merely in great emergencies, and the days when Saul could betake himself to his old pursuits on the Ephraim hills were past for ever. He must lead, and they must follow. The metaphor comes from the shepherd's usual place in the East, before his flock — our Lord uses the same image of sheep that follow his voice (John 10:27) — and Henry reaches for the picture too (Psalms 80:1). Wesley puts it as rule: he ruleth over you, and to him I have fully resigned my power. Gill sees a man in full possession of regal power, and draws a consequence: Samuel could now speak the more freely, since nobody could suspect him of hoping to be reinstated.

Ellicott hears some pathos in "I am old and grey-headed," and notices that it throws the elders' own words at Ramah back at them (1 Samuel 8:5): I am old, grown grey in your service — now listen while I ask what manner of service that has been, and whether anyone can find a flaw in it. Henry turns the age two ways: they were the more unkind to cast him off for it, and yet he was the more willing to resign, the weight of government lying heavy on his stooping shoulders; and being old he was the more able to advise them and the more entitled to be heard, since days shall speak and the multitude of years shall teach wisdom. Wesley reads it simply as incapacity: old, and therefore unable to bear the burden of government.

Where Samuel points at his sons, readings part. Clarke says it is generally agreed the words intimate that he had deprived them of their public employ and reduced them to the level of common people; Ellicott agrees that these sons, whose conduct as Samuel's deputies had drawn the elders' severest criticism, had been reduced, with their father's consent, to private citizens. Wesley has Samuel disclaim them outright: they are among you, private persons as you are; if they have injured any of you the law is now open, any of you may accuse them and your king can punish them, and I do not intercede for them. Henry presses the same point as an invitation to prosecute: they had not fled at the revolution, they stood as subjects of the new king like everyone else, and any wrong proved against them might be pursued by due course of law. But Ellicott relays a different reading from the Speaker's Commentary — that a tinge of mortified feeling at the rejection of himself and his family, mixed with a desire to recommend his sons to the nation's goodwill, may lie at the bottom of the mention.

The last clause asks Israel to review a life. Ellicott lists what was public knowledge: Samuel's early consecration to the sanctuary under peculiar and exceptional circumstances, the word of the LORD coming to him while still a boy, his recognition as a prophet directly afterwards, and his restless, unwearied work through the dark days after the fall of Shiloh. Now that they had virtually rejected his rule, he would have them think that life over and pronounce judgment on it. Clarke's verdict is short — a long, steady and immaculate servant of the public. Henry dates the beginning to the light of prophecy breaking on him early, from which time he began to be a burning and shining light to Israel; Wesley divides the office, partly a prophet's and partly a judge's.
3:
Samuel stands to be tried. Gill marks the reversal: no longer the supreme governor but a subject, accountable for any misdemeanour charged against him, now at their bar to be tried and judged. Wesley explains why — not out of ostentation but for his own just vindication, so the people might not afterwards reproach his government in defence of their own irregularities, and so that, publicly acquitted, he might more freely reprove their sins, particularly the sin of desiring a king when they had so little reason for it. Henry makes the same connection a rule: he that will with confidence tell another of his sin must see to it that he himself be clear.

The two witnesses Samuel summons occupy Ellicott at length. The old man speaks in a solemn presence — before the Eternal, looking up heavenward, and before His anointed, with a reverent gesture to the kingly form at his side. This, Ellicott notes, is the earliest instance of a king bearing that title of honour: in the early Hebrew story it is given now and again to the high priest, but henceforth it seems limited to the man invested with the kingly dignity. The charm the name carried for centuries he puts down to the fact that one greater than any of the sons of men would in the far future assume the same designation, His Anointed or His Christ, both translating the Hebrew Messiah; and for many a century, among all peoples, an awful curse has attached to anyone daring to lift his hand against the LORD's Anointed.

Why the challenge names an ox and an ass Ellicott explains from the economy. They are representative possessions in a primitive age, in a country where agriculture was the principal source of national resources: before David and Solomon there was comparatively little of the precious metals among a people who traded rarely abroad, and horses were unknown among them. The law names the ox and the ass in particular among the things an Israelite was forbidden to covet (Exodus 20:17). Henry itemises what Samuel disclaims: he had never distrained their cattle for tribute, fines or forfeitures, nor used their service without paying, nor taken bribes to pervert justice.

The word rendered bribe is literally a ransom, and Ellicott explains the practice — the gift, usually of money, by which a judge's favour was bought in the East, so that a criminal with means could often escape punishment. The point has an edge, since Samuel's own sons had taken bribes and perverted judgment (1 Samuel 8:3), and that accusation had been laid by the very elders before whom he was speaking. The old judge must have been very confident of his integrity to venture such a challenge; the elders were no respecters of persons and must have felt from his tone that reproaches were coming, yet they were constrained with one voice to witness that his long official life had been pure.

Clarke turns the scene into a question: did ever a minister of state anywhere resign his office with so much self-consciousness of integrity, backed by the universal approbation of the public? Clarke also finds a double role in the mention of the sons: as a minister of justice Samuel abandons them to their fate, having deprived them of their authority; as a tender father he indirectly and modestly pleads for them on the ground of his own services — can you forgive them for their father's sake? Henry adds what else the challenge secured: those who heard Samuel had been rejected would suspect he had done some evil thing, so it was needful that the record show he was laid aside not for any iniquity in his hands but to gratify a giddy people, who owned they could not have a better man to rule them and only desired a bigger one.
4:
The answer comes back as one voice. Gill allows either that one man spoke in the name of the rest or that they all cried out together; Keil and Delitzsch put the substance of it plainly — he had not done them any kind of injustice. Clarke turns it into a question: of what minister or governor can any nation under heaven say such things? Henry sorts the acquittal under two heads. They readily owned that Samuel had not made his government oppressive to them, nor used his power to their wrong; and that he had not made it expensive to them either, having taken nothing from any man's hand for the support of his dignity. Like Nehemiah he did not require the bread of the governor (Nehemiah 5:18) — not merely righteous but generous, having coveted no man's silver or gold or apparel (Acts 20:33). He did not expect them to do him honour at parting, Henry adds, and so mentioned none of his good services; all he asked was justice, and that they gave him.

Samuel then calls his witnesses a second time. Ellicott hears increased solemnity in it: the Eternal in the heavens above and His anointed king standing at his side are summoned to attest what the people had just acknowledged about his scrupulously just rule, and the assembly of Israel, again with one voice, shouted back that He is witness. Gill supplies the practical use of so formal a record — should they hereafter reproach and vilify him, and charge him with acts of corruption, injustice or violence.

But the witnesses are called against the people, and Keil and Delitzsch explain why that is not a slip. By the declaration they had just made about Samuel's judicial labours the people had condemned themselves: they had acknowledged on oath that there was no ground for dissatisfaction with his administration, and therefore no well-founded reason for their request for a king. The acquittal of the judge is the indictment of the nation.

One small feature of the Hebrew draws three answers. The verb introducing the people's reply stands in the singular where a plural is expected. Keil and Delitzsch take all Israel as the subject and judge the marginal reading "and they said," though simpler, by no means necessary. Ellicott relays a reading from the Talmud that makes the singular deliberate: Rabbi Elazer taught that on three occasions the Holy Spirit manifested himself in a peculiar manner — in the tribunal of Shem, in that of Samuel the Ramathite, and in that of Solomon — and here, where a plural was to be expected, it was the Holy Spirit that gave the answer, as the words assigning the living child to its mother were spoken by the Holy Spirit in Solomon's court (1 Kings 3:27). Henry draws a different comfort from the double testimony: the LORD is witness, who searcheth the heart, and his anointed is witness, who trieth overt acts — and the testimony of our neighbours, and especially of our own consciences, that we have in our places lived honestly, will be our comfort under the slights and contempts put upon us (3 John 1:12).
6:
With his own character cleared, Samuel turns to history. Gill marks the transition: having established his integrity, he proceeds to lay before the people some of the great things God had done for them formerly and down to the present time, the more to aggravate their ingratitude in rejecting God as their King. Henry notices what Samuel does not do — instead of upbraiding them with their unkindness to him, he sets himself to instruct them and keep them in the way of their duty, so that the change of government might be the less damage to them. The abstract of their national history that follows is given, Henry says, so that by weighing all he had done for them they might be for ever engaged to love him and serve him.

The verse's force turns on a word the English supplies. Ellicott would render the Hebrew "even the Eternal that advanced Moses and Aaron," and explains the dramatic situation: the elders had with one consent cried out "He is witness," and Samuel takes their words up again with great emphasis, so that the Authorised Version's rendering greatly weakens the force of the original. The Greek translators caught the thought accurately by supplying the word witness. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way — yea, the witness is Jehovah, who made Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt — but they are careful about the inference: the context by itself is enough to show that "is witness" is understood, so there is no reason to suppose the word has dropped out of the text through a copyist's error. The purpose of this renewed appeal, on their reading, was to bring the people to a still more thorough acknowledgment of their sin.

What "advanced" claims is also pressed. Keil and Delitzsch take the Hebrew verb for making in a moral and historical sense — to make a person what he is to be — and insist it has no connection with physical birth but relates simply to a man's introduction upon the stage of history, the Greek of the epistle using its own verb in the same way of Moses (Hebrews 3:2).

The Exodus is named first because of what it established. Ellicott observes that in these ancient records it is mentioned again and again as the great call of love by which the Eternal assumed the sovereignty over Israel — which is precisely what makes the request for a king an act of ingratitude. He then relays a comment of the Talmud on this verse taken together with the later list of deliverers: Scripture balances in the same scale the three least important personages with the three most important, to teach that Jerubbaal in his generation was like Moses in his, Bedan — said to be Samson — like Aaron, and Jephthah like Samuel; so that the most insignificant man, if appointed a ruler of the congregation, has the same authority as the most important.
7:
The command to stand still is read as a demand for attention. Gill has Samuel ask them to keep their place and not break up the assembly yet, but wait a little longer patiently and hearken with reverence to what he has further to say. Henry makes the posture itself significant — stand in token of reverence when God is speaking to you, stand still in token of attention and composedness of mind, and give me leave to reason with you.

Clarke catches the turn in one sentence: I have arraigned myself before God and you; I now arraign you before God. Ellicott expands the same movement into the speech Samuel might have made: we have advanced thus far in my solemn pleading, and my innocence as your judge you have borne witness to before God and the king — yet in spite of this you have wished to be quit of me, and of One who stood high above me, who has worked for you such mighty deeds. See now, ye elders, what this invisible King has done for your fathers and for you, whom ye have just deliberately replaced by an earthly king.

That Samuel proposes to reason rather than merely to command is what Henry fastens on. Religion has reason on its side (Isaiah 1:18), and the work of ministers is to reason with people — not only to exhort and direct but to persuade, to convince men's judgments and so to gain their wills and affections. Let reason rule men, Henry says, and they will be good.

What the "righteous acts" of the LORD include is where the readings diverge. Keil and Delitzsch define them as the benefits Jehovah had conferred on his people, understood as the results of his covenant fidelity, or as acts attesting his righteousness in fulfilling the covenant grace he had promised. Wesley renders the Hebrew plural as the righteousnesses, and takes them for mercies or benefits — the chief subject of the discourse that follows, in which the people's calamities are only briefly named, and that to illustrate God's mercy in their deliverances. Henry reads the phrase more widely, to take in both the benefits God bestowed in performance of his promises and the punishments he inflicted for their sins; the punishments are righteous acts no less than the favours, he argues, because in them God is just to his own honour (Judges 5:11).
8:
Whether the patriarch himself or his descendants are meant Gill leaves open. Jacob came down with his family to see his son Joseph and dwelt there; or rather, Gill thinks, his posterity are intended, who settled in Egypt, continued many years, and were at length oppressed by its people and brought into hard bondage. Henry keeps both ends of the story in view: into that house of bondage the family came down poor and little, and when the oppression grew heavy they cried unto God, who advanced Moses and Aaron from mean beginnings to be their deliverers and the founders of their state and settlement.

Ellicott marks the place of the verse in the argument. Samuel now rehearses, in order, the deeds of loving-kindness done for Israel by this Eternal King, beginning with the wonders of the Exodus and with the divine guidance that led them through so many dangers safe into Canaan — "this place." Keil and Delitzsch treat the same two items as the first proof of the righteous acts just announced: the rescue of the children of Israel out of Egypt, and their safe conduct into the promised land. A second proof is to follow, they add — the recovery of the nation from the power of the foes to whom the LORD had been obliged to give it up on account of its apostasy, worked through the judges he raised up whenever the people turned to him in penitence and cried for help. Clarke draws the pattern out of the whole history: God had ever raised up deliverers when their necessities required such interference.

The phrase "this place," and the share the two leaders had in bringing Israel to it, exercise Wesley at length. It means this land, he says, and they are credited with settling the nation there for several reasons together: they brought the people in and seated them in part of it, the portion outside Jordan; they were, under God, the principal authors of the entry itself, having led them out of Egypt and conducted them across the wilderness, so that their prayers above and their counsel below preserved Israel from ruin; they issued the divine command for apportioning the territory, and encouraged the tribes to go in; and lastly Moses put Joshua in his own room and charged him to plant them there, which he did.
9:
Forgetting is the word, and Gill narrows it: the Targum reads it as forgetting the worship of the LORD their God, so that what is meant is a fall into idolatry — for those who neglect his worship and serve idols may truly be said to have forgotten him. Wesley makes the forgetting active rather than passive: they revolted from him and carried themselves as if they had wholly forgotten his innumerable favours. Ellicott takes the same view of what idolatry is in this argument — simply an act of rebellion against the pure government of the invisible King, attended as it always was by immorality and shameless wickedness, and punished by the withdrawal of the divine protection.

Wesley sees a retort buried in the verse. An objector might say the people asked for a king because under the judges they lived at great uncertainties and were often exercised with sharp afflictions. Samuel concedes that they were; but he adds, by way of retortion, that they were themselves the cause of it by forgetting God — so the fault lay not in that kind of government but in their transgressing the rules of it. Henry presses the cost of it in their own terms: they enslaved themselves, being sold like criminals and captives into the hand of oppressors, and exposed themselves to the desolation of war, their neighbours fighting against them.

The three oppressors named are not in order, and Ellicott says so: they are prominent instances quoted as they occurred to the speaker, without careful attention to the sequence of events and times, which his argument did not require. The three leading neighbouring nations allowed for a season to harass the tribes of God's inheritance are the Canaanites, the Philistines and the Moabites. Hazor appears in the records as the capital city of the Canaanites and again as a royal residence (Joshua 11:1; Judges 4:2), and Sisera is named as the well-known commander of the army Israel fought, and as the victim of the sanguinary but patriotic deed of fury of Jael. Keil and Delitzsch identify the oppression the same way, as that of the Canaanite king of Hazor whose captain Sisera was, and Clarke simply refers the reader to the transactions in the book of Judges. The king of Moab, Ellicott adds, is Eglon, whom Ehud slew.

On the Philistines Ellicott enlarges. They dwelt literally among the Israelites and were the most formidable of their foes for a long series of years, their many strongholds and fastnesses comparable to the robber nests that in the stormy middle ages disturbed the peace and scourged the commerce of Central Europe. It was owing especially to them that Israel made such slow progress in wealth and the arts of civilisation for so long; and the advance of the nation from the days of Samuel, who first really checked them, was singularly rapid — in an almost incredibly short period a poor and half-barbarous people became highly cultured, wealthy and powerful, in great measure through the complete subjugation of the Philistines under Samuel, Saul and David.
10: The crying out is read as the turn of the cycle. Gill places it when they were in the hands of their enemies, in bondage and cruelly oppressed; Ellicott makes the response immediate — as soon as they were convinced of their sin and rebellion, accused themselves and returned to their old allegiance, their invisible King, ever full of pity and tender compassion, forgave them and sent quick deliverance. On the gods they confess to having served, Ellicott notes that Baal and Ashtaroth were the leading Phoenician deities, their worship imported with most of its details probably from Carthage, where the temple of the Sun god was renowned in that luxurious and splendid city; Ashtaroth is the Greek Astarte, and the pair were probably worshipped originally as simply the sun and moon, the plural forms pointing to the various personifications and titles of god and goddess. Henry turns the fathers' confession into a warning to their children: let them not imitate the sins of their fathers, for what those had done amiss they had many a time wished undone again — and let the children reckon that good at all times which their fathers found good in bad times.
11:
Two of the four names are secure. Gill and Clarke both identify Jerubbaal with Gideon, Gill noting from the Targum that it was the name given him when he first became a judge; Ellicott explains the surname as one given out of scorn and derision for the Phoenician deity — let Baal then strive or contend with me. Jephthah needs no gloss, and Henry puts him with Gideon as great conquerors in their time.

Bedan is the chapter's hardest word, and the proposals are many. Ellicott observes that the name occurs nowhere in the record of the judges; the only Bedan elsewhere is a descendant of Machir the Manassite, apparently a person of no importance (1 Chronicles 7:17). The two most ancient versions, the Greek and the Syriac, read Barak instead, and Ellicott thinks the substitution probable, the letters forming the two names in Hebrew being very similar, so that a scribe might easily have written one for the other; Clarke reports the same reading from the Syriac and Arabic, and adds that the catalogue of heroes in the epistle connects Barak with Gideon and Jephthah (Hebrews 11:32).

Against Barak stands Samson. The Targum reads him here, and Clarke says many commentators are of that opinion. Rabbi Kimchi, whom Ellicott cites, suggests Bedan is written for Ben-Dan, the son of Dan the Danite, that is Samson, and Henry reports the same, adding that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him in Dan, in the camp of Dan. God's raising so eminent a saviour out of so obscure a tribe, Wesley adds, left Israel no reason to distrust him.

A third candidate is Jair. Clarke says Calmet thinks Jair is intended, who judged Israel twenty-two years (Judges 10:3), and Wesley prefers that identification on two grounds: it agrees better with the time and order of the judges, since Jair came before Jephthah where Samson came after him, and it agrees better with other scripture, since among the sons of an earlier Jair we meet with one called Bedan — a name that may have been given to Jair the judge to distinguish him from that first one. Henry reports Jair as the view of the learned Mr. Poole, but offers a possibility of his own first: Bedan may have been some eminent person who was an instrument of salvation though not recorded in the book of Judges, like the Shamgar of whom it is said that he delivered Israel but not that he judged them (Judges 3:31), who perhaps guarded one side of the country while another judge acted on the other. Ellicott notes that Wordsworth, curiously, prefers to leave the unknown name standing, arguing that in its very obscurity we have a confirmation of the speech's genuineness, since a forger would not have ventured to insert a name occurring nowhere else.

The last name is the speaker's own, and that too has been altered. The Syriac and Arabic substitute Samson for Samuel, finding a difficulty in a man quoting himself, and Clarke thinks it most natural to suppose Samuel does not mention himself here. But Ellicott answers that the other versions uniformly agree with the Hebrew, and that Samuel could well cite himself as a signal instance of God's loving pity, conscious as he was of his own high mission: no judge had accomplished such great things for the people, and none had received more general recognition, so it was a most fitting name to close the list. Henry makes the same defence on different ground — Samuel mentions himself not to his own praise but to the honour of God, who had made him an instrument of subduing the Philistines. Wesley takes the closing words about dwelling safe as the sting of the whole recital: it was no necessity but mere wantonness that made them desire a change.
12:
Nahash is the occasion, and Gill sets the contrast sharply: for all the Lord's kindness in raising up judge after judge to deliver them whenever they cried, the moment they perceived the Ammonite preparing war they did not apply to the Lord for protection but asked for a king to go before them and fight their battles. Henry has the same sequence with the exchange filled in — Nahash threatened them, they asked Samuel to nominate a general, and he told them God was commander-in-chief in all their wars and they needed no other, since what was wanting in them would be made up by his power. The LORD is your king; but they insisted, Nay, but a king shall reign over us. Wesley presses the aggravation: God was then their immediate king and governor, both able and willing to deliver them if they had cried to him, as they and their ancestors had plentiful experience, so that they did not at all need another — and the desire for one was a manifest reproach against God.

The history behind the demand gets two refinements. Clarke notes that this was not the first time they had asked for a king (1 Samuel 8:5), but at this crisis they became more importunate, and in consequence the kingdom was a second time confirmed to Saul — elected at Mizpeh, confirmed at Gilgal. Ellicott thinks it has been suggested with great probability that Nahash and the Ammonites had invaded the trans-Jordanic territory in the period immediately before the demand, and that the invasion which culminated in the siege of Jabesh-gilead was only one of a series of destructive forays.

How far the king was the people's own choice is the question the next verse raises. Gill holds both ends: God chose their king for them, but at their request, and they approved, consented to and confirmed the choice he had made, so that it was in effect their own. Wesley offers the same two senses — they chose generally, in that they chose that form of government, or particularly, in that they approved God's choice and confirmed it. Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew word order as deciding it against the people: the word for choosing by lot stands before "whom ye asked for" precisely to show that the demand was the strongest act they could perform, since they had not merely chosen a king with Samuel's consent or at his direction but had demanded one of their own self-will.

What the doubled "behold" does is also noticed. Keil and Delitzsch take the second one to bring out still more strongly that Jehovah had fulfilled the people's desire — their request had been an act of hostility to God, and yet he granted it. Ellicott hears the turn from past to present in it: you now have your wish, behold your king, the Eternal has seen fit to grant your petition, and his election rests on the will of that invisible King whom you have virtually rejected. Henry balances the two sides of the gift in a phrase: a king of your own asking, which is to your shame, but a king of God's making, which is to his honour and the glory of his grace — for God did not cast them off even when they in effect cast him off. Wesley puts the concession more bluntly still: he hath yielded to your inordinate desire.
14:
Gill begins with the first of the four conditions, and makes it the root of the rest: all worship and service of God, and all obedience to his word and ordinances, should spring from fear and reverence of him, which is why the whole of worship, external and internal alike, is sometimes expressed simply as the fear of the LORD. Clarke states the bargain in a sentence — on condition that they rebel no more, God will take them and their king under his merciful protection, and he and his kingdom shall be confirmed and continued.

Where the sentence ends, however, is disputed, and the dispute decides what is being promised. Keil and Delitzsch read the last clause as the apodosis — if ye will only fear the LORD and serve him, then ye as well as the king who rules over you will be after Jehovah your God — and defend it on two grounds: the Hebrew particle in the sense of "if only" needs no apodosis at all, being virtually equivalent to the wish "O that ye would only!", and nothing has to be supplied to the closing words, since to be after a person is good Hebrew and frequently met with, particularly of attaching oneself to a king. Ellicott says flatly that the English Version has missed the point of the original, and would render it: if ye will fear the LORD, and if both ye and the king that reigneth over you will follow the LORD your God, it shall be well with you. He quotes Dean Payne Smith for the effect — Samuel piled up one condition upon another and then, from the depth of his emotion, broke off, leaving the blessed consequences of their obedience unsaid — and finds the same unfinished construction in a saying of our Lord, where the apodosis is likewise left to be supplied (Luke 19:42).

Whether the clause states a duty or confers a privilege divides Wesley from Henry. Wesley insists it is a privilege and not a duty: God shall still go before them as he has hitherto done, as leader and governor, to direct, protect and deliver, and he will not forsake them though they have given him just cause to do so — the phrase of going after the LORD does sometimes signify a man's obedience, but here it is set against the threatening of the next verse, so it marks something received upon the performance of duty rather than the duty itself. Henry will not separate the two. The promise means both that they shall continue in the way of their duty, which will be their honour and comfort, and that they shall continue under divine guidance and protection — for following God is a work that is its own wages, the matter of a promise as well as of a precept, and those who follow him faithfully will be divinely strengthened to continue following him. The LORD is with you, Henry adds, while you are with him.
15:
The threat that answers the promise reaches back rather than forward. Keil and Delitzsch note that the comparison with the fathers is very suitable here, because the people were looking to a king for the removal of all the calamities that had fallen on them from time immemorial; and the Greek version's paraphrase, which turns the fathers into "your king," they call a very unhappy conjecture, though Thenius would alter the Hebrew to suit it. Ellicott judges the English translation, with several of the versions behind it, accurate and happy in taking the Hebrew comparatively — as it was against your fathers — and he lists the alternatives it sets aside: Rabbi Kimchi prefers to read "fathers" as standing for "kings," so that the hand of the LORD shall be against them and their kings, while the Greek has simply "against you and your king." Keil and Delitzsch defend the comparative sense on a point of usage, noting that the Hebrew conjunction is most often used that way before whole sentences, and that its use here is explicable because the two words rendered "as upon your fathers" carry the force of an entire sentence.

What the warning destroys is the hope that had produced the king. Wesley identifies the fathers as those who lived under the judges, and draws the conclusion: they shall have no advantage by the change of government, nor shall their kings be able to protect them against God's displeasure. Henry puts the same thought as a refusal of the bargain they imagined they had struck — do not think that having a king will secure you against God's judgments, or that having in this one instance made yourselves like the nations you may sin at as cheap a rate as they do; the hand of the LORD will be against you, as it was against your fathers when they offended him in the days of the judges. We mistake, he says, if we think we can evade God's justice by shaking off his dominion: if God shall not rule us, yet he will judge us. Gill adds only that the rebellion contemplated is theirs and their king's together, by disregarding the LORD's precepts, both affirmative and negative.
16:
The command to stand is not about posture. Gill says it respects not so much the position of their bodies as the fixed attention of their minds; Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew the same way, taking "place yourselves" as an instruction to make themselves ready, inserted between the opening words and the thing to be seen in order to fix the people's attention more closely on the miracle as an event of great importance, and one they ought to lay to heart. Henry notices the change from the earlier summons: Samuel had told them to stand and hear, but seeing that his reasoning had not reached them — so stupid were they and unthinking — he now bids them stand and see. If what he said in a still small voice did not touch their hearts, nor his doctrine which dropped as the dew, they shall hear God speaking in dreadful claps of thunder and the great rain of his strength. Ellicott puts the summons in Samuel's own voice: stand forth, ye elders, and I will show you by a voice from heaven that this very asking for a king, though the Eternal has granted your prayer, is evil in his sight.

What the sign is to prove is the harder matter, since the request had been granted. Keil and Delitzsch find the chain of thought in the phrase "yea, even now": even now, with the king standing before them, they may see that they acted very wickedly in the sight of Jehovah in demanding one. Clarke's gloss on the great thing is simply that it was an unusual occurrence.

Henry explains why the point needed making at all, and in doing so diagnoses the mood of the assembly. They were at that moment rejoicing before God in and with their king, and offering him the sacrifices of praise, which they hoped he would accept; and this perhaps made them think there was no harm in asking a king, but that they had really done well in it. Samuel therefore charges it upon them as their sin, as wickedness, great wickedness in the sight of the LORD. Though we meet with prosperity and success in a way of sin, Henry warns, we must not therefore think the more favourably of it. They have a king, and if they conduct themselves well that king may be a very great blessing to them, and yet Samuel will have them perceive that their wickedness was great in asking for him — for we must never think well of what God in his law frowns upon, however in his providence he may seem to smile upon it.

Ellicott measures the act against what it displaced. Their wishing for an earthly king was the crown of a long course of rebellion against the Supreme will; it was, in fact, the breaking up for ever of the glorious ideal which had been so long before the eyes of the noblest spirits in Israel.
17:
The question about the season is the hinge of the sign, and the witnesses agree on the climate while differing on the calendar. Clarke takes the harvest to have commenced about the end of June or the beginning of July, citing Jerome, who spent several years in the promised land and says in so many words that he never saw rain in those provinces, and especially in Judea, at that time of year. Gill reports the same testimony from Jerome, who lived long in those parts, and adds Rabbi Joseph Kimchi's flat statement that in the land of Israel rain never fell all the days of harvest. Ellicott dates the Canaan wheat harvest earlier, between the middle of May and the middle of June, and puts the climate more carefully: rain in that season seldom or never falls, but if it does it is usually severe — the testimony, he says, of one who spoke as a resident, confirmed by the observations of the latest travellers and scholars. Wesley says only that thunder or rain was a rare thing in those parts at that time, the weather being more constant in its seasons there than it is with us.

Gill presses the detail of that particular day. Rain in Judea fell usually only twice a year, in what are called the former and the latter rain, and through the months from spring to autumn it was not usual for any to fall at all. But Samuel's question, he argues, points at more than the season in general: on that very day the men were out in the fields reaping the wheat, so the sky cannot have been cloudy or inclining to rain but must have been serene and clear, or they would not have been employed in cutting down the corn — all of which made the case the more remarkable.

What turns weather into a sign is the notice given beforehand. Henry grants that thunder and rain have natural causes and sometimes terrible effects, but says Samuel made it appear that this was designed by the almighty power of God on purpose to convince them: not only by its coming at an unusual time, in wheat harvest and on a fair clear day when no sign of a storm appeared, but by his announcing it in advance. He appealed to it as a sign — I will call upon the LORD, and he will send thunder, and send it now, to confirm the word of his servant and to make you see that I spoke truly when I told you God was angry with you for asking a king. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the effect: a terrible storm of rain with thunder, at a season when such storms rarely took place, coming as it did in direct answer to the seer's invocation, struck the people naturally with great fear.

Wesley states the two things the rain was meant to teach: that God was displeased with them, and how foolishly and wickedly they had done in rejecting the government of that God at whose command are all things both in heaven and in earth. Keil and Delitzsch call the result a salutary terror.
18:
How Samuel called is worth noticing. Gill insists it was not in an authoritative way or by way of command but by prayer, and points to the Targum, which renders the previous verse "I will pray before the LORD." Henry has the answer arrive before the petition was finished — even while he was yet speaking, the LORD sent thunder and rain — and draws two conclusions from it: what a powerful influence God has upon this earth, that he could of a sudden, when natural causes did not work towards it, bring such rain and thunder out of his treasures (Psalms 135:7); and what a powerful interest Samuel had in heaven, that God would hearken to the voice of a man (Joshua 10:14) and answer him in the secret place of thunder (Psalms 81:7). That son of prayer, Henry adds, was still famous for success in prayer. Clarke calls the thing a most evident miracle, since it was totally unusual and came at Samuel's call.

The weapon chosen carries its own message. Henry recalls that God had testified his displeasure in exactly this way once before, and at Samuel's prayer too, when he discomfited the Philistines with a great thunder (1 Samuel 7:10); now that Israel had rebelled and vexed his Holy Spirit he turned to be their enemy and fought against them with the weapons lately employed against their adversaries (Isaiah 63:10). Wesley draws the comparison the storm was meant to force: God showed them their folly in desiring a king to save them rather than God or Samuel, expecting more from an arm of flesh than from the arm of God or the power of prayer — could their king thunder with a voice like God, or their prince command such forces as the prophet could by his prayers? And however serene their condition seemed now, like the weather in wheat harvest, if God pleased he could soon change the face of their heavens.

The fear that followed was double. Clarke says they dreaded God's terrible majesty and feared Samuel too, perceiving that he had so much power with God; Wesley says the same of the prophet's power and favour. Henry finds the correction in it: when they had a king they were ready to think they must fear him only, and God made them know that he himself is greatly to be feared, and his prophets for his sake — they had been rejoicing in their king, and God taught them to rejoice with trembling.
19:
The confession was unanimous and immediate. Gill places it during the tempest and in the midst of it, the general cry of the people, who were unanimous in it. Clarke explains the panic behind it: knowing that they had rebelled against God, they saw they had everything to fear from his justice and his power. Henry notes the timing from the prophet's side: he did not extort the avowal until the matter was settled and the king confirmed, lest it look as though he aimed rather at establishing himself in the government than at bringing them to amendment. Clarke is careful about what they confessed: it is no sin to have a king, and a good king is one of the greatest blessings of God's providence, but it is a sin to put a man in the place of God.

Clarke alone distrusts the contrition. Is it not strange, he asks, that they did not now attempt to repair their fault? They might have done it and did not; they owned the fault but did not put it away — which is the general way of mankind, content to bear the character of sinner and heedless of what follows. Henry reads the same moment more charitably, observing only that some are never brought to see their guilt by milder means than storms and thunders, and that in begging Samuel's prayers they saw their need of the man they had lately slighted: many who will not have Christ to reign over them would yet be glad to have him intercede for them. Why they did not pray for themselves both he and Wesley explain from the words they used — they could not expect God to hear their own prayers, and could not call him theirs — Wesley puts their words as a confession in themselves, that they were ashamed and afraid to call him their God, while Samuel had so great an interest in him — so they asked the prophet to improve that interest on their behalf. Keil and Delitzsch note what the request drew out of him: an announcement that the LORD would not forsake his people for his great name's sake, if only they would serve him with uprightness.
20:
What kind of fear is forbidden is the first question, and the answers narrow it carefully. Gill takes it of the immediate terror — fear not being destroyed by the tempest. Wesley makes it a desponding fear, as if there were no hope left for them. Henry puts the distinction at its sharpest: Samuel would not have the terrors of the LORD frighten them away from him, since they were intended to frighten them to him, so that "fear not" means do not despair, do not fear with amazement, for the weather will clear up after the storm.

Clarke reads the concessive clause as a pardon with a condition attached: although ye have done all this wickedness, what was past God would pass by, provided they would be obedient in future. Keil and Delitzsch are anxious that the comfort not be overread. In order to give no encouragement to a false trust in the covenant faithfulness of the LORD, Samuel followed the words "fear not" by telling them again, very decidedly, that they had done wrong — and then that they were nevertheless not to turn away from the LORD but to serve him with all their heart. Henry guards the same ground from the other side: every transgression in the covenant, though it displease the LORD, does not throw us out of covenant, and therefore God's just rebukes must not drive us from our hope in his mercy.

Ellicott finds a whole gospel in the sentence. A very great and precious evangelical truth is contained in these comforting words, which show how deeply this eminent servant of the Most High had entered into the Eternal thought: no sin or course of sin was too great to be repented of. Afar off, and perhaps in a glass darkly, such ministers of the LORD saw the Lamb of God whose blood cleanseth from all sin. Isaiah pressed the same truth home on the sinning Israel of his own day, that though their sins were as scarlet they should be white as snow; Samuel's bidding the people, in spite of the guilty past, press on and follow the LORD and serve him with all the heart was taken up by his prophet-successors and repeated in coming ages in such exhortations as "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God" (Hosea 14:1); and it was re-echoed by men like Paul, who bade their hearers forget the things behind, their past guilt and failure, and press on fearlessly for the real prize of life.
21:
Ellicott begins with a textual objection that changes the shape of the sentence. The passage is more forcible, he says, without the "for" and the words the English translation supplies in italics; the verse would then run simply "Turn ye not aside after vain things which cannot profit." Singularly enough, not one of the ancient versions renders the Hebrew particle at all — they all omit it — from which he concludes that it has got into the text through some copyist's error since the versions were made.

What the vain things are nobody doubts. Gill takes the turning aside to be a desertion of God's worship, and reads the threatened consequence as following upon that desertion and upon no other; Wesley names idols outright, and adds that Israel had often turned to them before and, notwithstanding this warning, did so again afterwards. Both he and Henry gloss the word itself: idols are called vain things elsewhere (Deuteronomy 32:21; Jeremiah 2:5) and are such, being mere nothings with no power in them, no influence upon us, and no use or benefit to us. Clarke finds a sharper echo, noting that the word here is the one used of the earth before it was formed — waste, empty and formless — so that idols are confusion and things of naught, an idol being nothing in the world and the representative of no intelligent being (Genesis 1:2). Henry turns the same point on the reader: whatever you turn aside to, you will find it a vain thing that can never answer your expectations and will certainly deceive you if you trust it — a broken reed, a broken cistern, unable to profit those who sought to it in their wants or to deliver those who sought to it in their straits, being vain, and not what they pretended to be (1 Corinthians 8:4). Keil and Delitzsch read the repetition of the prohibition as deliberate reinforcement of the admonition just given, with an explanation attached to it: in turning away from the LORD the people would be falling away to things that could bring them neither help nor deliverance.
22:
The ground of the promise that follows is God's own name, and each voice spells out what that protects. Gill argues from the reputation at stake: should God forsake his people and suffer them to come to ruin, his name would be blasphemed among the heathen, and he would be charged with want of power to help them, or want of faithfulness to his promise, or inconstancy, or want of affection for them. Keil and Delitzsch define the name as the great one he had acquired in the sight of all the nations by the marvellous guidance of Israel thus far, now to be preserved against misapprehension and blasphemy (Joshua 7:9). Wesley says the same and draws the practical use: God alleges this reason to take them off from all conceit of their own merit, and to assure them that even if they did truly repent of all their sins and serve him with all their heart, their salvation would still not be due to their merits but be the effect of his free mercy.

How far that makes the promise unconditional is the live question. Keil and Delitzsch put the emphasis on the pronoun — his people is what the Israelites could only be while they proved themselves such by serving Jehovah with all their heart. Clarke reads the assurance as a reprieve rather than a guarantee: he will not as yet cast you off, though you have deserved it, because his purpose in preserving them in their land and religion was not yet accomplished — and even that was not for their sake but for his own great name's sake, God drawing his reasons from himself. Wesley leaves the people one way to forfeit it: he will not forsake you, except you thrust him away. Henry argues the other way, from the freeness of the choice to its fixedness — had God chosen them for their good merits we might fear he would cast them off for their bad merits, but choosing them for his name's sake, for his name's sake he will not leave them. Ellicott simply names the doctrine: this is election, resting so far as we can see on the arbitrary will of God, though deep reasons no doubt exist for every seemingly arbitrary choice, as the analogy of everyday life teaches when one vessel is made to honour and another to dishonour — things inscrutable to us.
23:
Samuel answers more than was asked, and Henry counts the ways. He might have said, go to Saul, the king you put in my room, and get him to pray for you; but so far is he from upbraiding their disrespect that he promises more than they asked. They asked it of him as a favour, and he undertakes it as a duty, startling at the very thought of neglect — pray for you! God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in not doing it. It is a sin against God, Henry adds, not to pray for the Israel of God, and good men are afraid of the guilt of omissions. They asked prayer for this occasion, and he promised to continue it while he lived: our rule is to pray without ceasing, and we sin if we restrain prayer, and in particular if we cease praying for the church. And they asked only prayer, while he promised teaching too — though unwilling to be under his government as a judge, they would not for that be denied his instruction as a prophet.

Gill reads the verse as a double pardon. As Samuel had given them reason to believe God would pardon their sin in rejecting him as King, so he likewise forgave their offence against himself in rejecting him as governor under God, so that they need fear neither with a servile fear; and as God would still be gracious if they abode by his service, so Samuel would do them every good office in his power. Clarke recalls what they had begged — that they might not die — and reports the reply as a confession: he would consider himself a sinner should he cease to be their intercessor.

Both Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott illustrate it from the same quotation: in this Samuel sets a glorious example to all rulers, who should not be led astray by the ingratitude of their subjects, nor give up on that account all interest in their welfare, but persevere the more in their anxiety for them. Ellicott adds a note from Gregory, that Jeremiah especially brings forward Moses and Samuel as men of extraordinary power with God (Jeremiah 15:1) — and why? because they prayed for their enemies.

Ellicott reads the promise to teach against the constitutional change just made. The old man felt that although his powers as judge were not yet abrogated, there would be little opportunity to exercise them: before the regular authority of a king surrounded by armed men, such authority as he had wielded over the hearts of Israel must fall into abeyance. But one higher office remained untouched — that of prophet — and in that sphere he would work ceaselessly on while he lived. The words he used tell out to all ages, Ellicott says, that the true function of the prophet is to teach the people the good and the right way; and Samuel's own life of brave self-denial showed that such teaching must be pressed home by something more than words.

On the way itself Clarke and Henry arrive together. Clarke takes Samuel to be promising to show them what true religion is — the way to happiness and heaven, right because there is no crookedness in it and good because there is no evil in it. Henry argues they might be sure of no other way from him, since the right way is certainly the good way, the way of duty being the way of pleasure and profit. Ellicott closes with Ewald's judgement: only a Samuel could quit office so, challenging all to convict him of one single injustice in his past career, and by resigning gaining rather than losing greatness — no longer judge and ruler but simple prophet, able now to discourse with greater freedom of the monarchy about to be introduced.
24:
The fear now required is the opposite of the one forbidden a few verses earlier, and Gill and Henry both mark the turn. Gill distinguishes it from the servile fear Samuel has just dissuaded: this is a filial fear, a reverential affection for God, taking in the whole of religious worship, internal and external. Henry puts the two side by side — fear not, with a slavish fear; but fear the LORD, with a filial fear — and makes service the fruit and evidence of it, in the duties of worship and of a godly conversation, in truth and sincerity and not in show and profession only, with the heart and with all the heart, not dissembling and not dividing.

Clarke unpacks each term of the charge in turn. To fear is to know, respect and reverence him; to serve is to consider him Lord and Master and oneself his servant; in truth is to be ever honest and sincere; with all the heart is to have every affection engaged in the work of obedience, acting not merely from a principle of duty but from a pious and affectionate sense of obligation — towards God as an affectionate child acts towards a tender and loving parent. Wesley states the alternative bluntly: otherwise neither Samuel's prayers nor his counsels will stand them in any stead, which is Gill's point too.

What the great things are that they must consider is where Keil and Delitzsch part from the rest. They take the reference to be not the thunder and rain granted at Samuel's prayer but the giving of a king — the very thing the people had sinned in asking is named as the mercy they are to weigh. Clarke casts the net wider: review the history of your fathers, review your own life, and see what interpositions of power, mercy, goodness and truth God has displayed on your behalf, loading you daily with his benefits. Henry makes the consideration one of two motives, binding them in gratitude to serve God.

The second motive is interest, and the chapter ends on it. Henry has the threat touch the thing they were proudest of: you shall be destroyed by the judgments of God, both you and your king, of whom you expect so much, and who will be a blessing to you if you keep in with God. Gill specifies the wickedness contemplated — continuing to rebel, revolting from God, departing from his worship, despising his prophets and serving idols. Clarke makes it a complete reckoning: if ye do wickedly you shall be destroyed, your kingdom destroyed, your king destroyed, so that life and good, death and evil were set plainly before them. Never was a people more fully warned, he says, and never did a people profit less by the warning — and he turns the warning on his own reader, asking what he is, and whether he too is such a monument of God's justice and forbearance. Henry's last word is about the speaker rather than the hearers: thus, as a faithful watchman, Samuel gave them warning, and so delivered his own soul.
